newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma sanctions may deter Western firms, not Asia.
newsitem.headline: Burma sanctions may deter Western firms, not Asia.

text.p: A U.S. ban on new investment in Burma is likely to deter some Western firms from doing business there, but analysts said strong interest from Asian nations would insulate the country's impoverished economy from collapse.

The sanctions -- which Washington said it imposed because of Burma's dismal human rights record -- apply only to U.S. firms, but are likely to influence other Western companies, diplomats and analysts said on Wednesday.
Western investors were already wary about political and economic stability in Burma and the U.S. decision could lead some to decide the risk was too great, they said.
"It will certainly worry a lot of people," said one diplomat. "Political risk has raised. Companies will see pretty quickly a next step (by the U.S.) would be total disinvestment."
The International Monetary Fund recently said Burma's poor economic fundamentals, mainly the legacy of more than 25 years of central planning, had hindered progress.
It said the nation's military leaders had to adopt a sweeping reform programme to put the economy back on track.

But Burma's fledgling economy was not expected to collapse because of the U.S. sanctions since Asian companies which have been aggressively investing in the country over the past few years were not expected to pull out, analysts said.
"It's not going to have that much immediate effect on the economy, but it will put off potential investors, especially Western investors," said one Rangoon-based diplomat.
"What you may see though is the Asian investors taking the place of U.S. firms," said another diplomat. "In this part of the world, people tend to be very pragmatic."

Bruce Gale, Singapore-based regional analyst at Political & Economic Risk Consultancy, said: "I suppose it (the ban) would be a disappointment for American companies based in Singapore who (are) looking at possibly going into Burma. But I don't see that it will affect ASEAN businessmen."
Southeast Asian nations such as Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia have been building up investment in Burma.

Since Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) opened up the economy after it seized power in 1988, it has approved about $2.7 billion worth of projects from those three countries, the latest official figures show.
Total approved foreign investment in Burma from late 1988 through March 31 this year amounts to about $6.05 billion. Around 50 percent of that has actually been invested, diplomats said.
Asian reaction to the sanctions, especially among members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), was muted.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said the sanctions would not delay the entry of Burma into ASEAN, which is expected later this year.
"We're going to work very hard to get Myanmar (Burma) into ASEAN," he added.
Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said the sanctions would not affect trade with Thailand and that the U.S. ban should not have any impact on plans to admit Burma into ASEAN.
"We understand the Washington position...but ASEAN has its own approach and we would continue with our constructive engagement policy," Chavalit told reporters.

ASEAN, which comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, follows a policy of "constructive engagement" and says Burma's economy will only suffer more if it is isolated.
"The Americans are sensitive about the situation in Burma but for us Asians, we are different, and I still believe that there will be change in Burma and the situation will improve," Chavalit added.
Vietnam said the imposition of sanctions against Burma amounted to an interference in the internal affairs of a nation.
Other nations in the region, such as Japan and Australia, have said they do not plan to impose sanctions but would try to persuade Burma's generals to move towards democracy.
